options: A backup archive kept for disaster recovery
A collection of unorganised or unprocessed data waiting to be sorted, analysed or managed
A dataset that has been fully cleansed and catalogued
A database index that has become corrupted
A report showing which datasets were deleted
questions.explanation: A data doom pile is a virtual space where unorganised or unprocessed data accumulates before it is properly sorted, cleansed, processed or analysed.

questions.stem: The data doom pile is compared to which everyday physical space?
options: A locked filing cabinet
A library catalogue
A junk drawer or cluttered area for miscellaneous items
A bank vault
A museum display case
questions.explanation: Just as people keep a junk drawer or cluttered area for miscellaneous items, data doom piles are repositories, folders or databases where unstructured or unprocessed data accumulates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is given as an example of a data doom pile?
options: A spreadsheet of survey responses that has not yet been analysed or organised
A published research paper with its findings
A photo album carefully sorted by year
A completed report card with verified grades
An indexed database with documented schemas
questions.explanation: Unprocessed survey responses sitting in a spreadsheet before analysis are one of the examples of a data doom pile; the other options describe already-organised outputs.

questions.stem: A student's email inbox holds many emails with attachments and links, some important and some not, all waiting to be categorised, archived or deleted. How is this inbox described in the data doom pile concept?
options: As a data warehouse
As a governance framework
As a data catalogue
As a data doom pile
As a data lake
questions.explanation: Uncategorised emails in an inbox are used as a relatable example of a data doom pile: information that has accumulated without yet being sorted or managed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the examples used to illustrate a data doom pile?
options: Unsorted data files in a computer folder
Raw data from science experiments
Unprocessed sensor readings
Images in an unorganised gallery
A fully labelled and filed set of tax returns
questions.explanation: Unsorted files, raw experiment data, unprocessed sensor readings and unorganised photo galleries are all listed examples. A fully labelled, filed set of documents is the opposite of a doom pile.

questions.stem: Why is it important to address a data doom pile?
options: Because unprocessed data automatically deletes itself after a period
Because ignoring it can lead to missed opportunities, lost insights and difficulty locating particular information when needed
Because storage providers charge only for organised data
Because raw data cannot legally be stored
Because doom piles cause hardware failures
questions.explanation: Organising and analysing data is crucial for informed decisions; ignoring the doom pile can mean ignored opportunities, missed insights and trouble finding specific information.

questions.stem: Which of these is a recommended way to address a data doom pile?
options: Delete all unprocessed data immediately
Move the data to a second unorganised folder
Implement an organising system such as folders, naming conventions or tagging
Wait until the pile stops growing before acting
Restrict access so nobody can view the data
questions.explanation: The recommended approaches are to implement a system for organising data (folders, naming conventions, tagging), schedule regular review times, and use analysis tools to extract insights.

questions.stem: In an engineering project, readings collected from several sensors have not yet been processed or interpreted. What does this dataset represent?
options: A data doom pile awaiting analysis
A finished data product
A governance policy
A data quality standard
A technology roadmap
questions.explanation: Unprocessed sensor readings are one of the examples of a data doom pile: collected data that is waiting for processing and interpretation.

questions.stem: What role does scheduling regular review times play in managing a data doom pile?
options: It makes data collection unnecessary
It helps prevent the accumulation of unorganised data
It converts raw data into images
It replaces the need for naming conventions
It guarantees the data is accurate
questions.explanation: Scheduling regular times to review and process unorganised data is recommended specifically to prevent accumulation of the doom pile.

questions.stem: The data doom pile idea is compared to cleaning up a physical space. What is the point of this comparison?
options: That data should be printed out and stored physically
That physical clutter and data clutter are unrelated problems
That organising and analysing data, like tidying a space, makes it more functional and supports informed decisions
That only physical spaces need tidying
That data doom piles are always caused by hardware
questions.explanation: Just as cleaning a physical space makes it more functional, organising and analysing data is crucial for making informed decisions.
